description: Hi! I’m Eman, a full-stack developer skilled in Python, FastAPI, APIs, databases, React, Next.js, and AI integrations. I enjoy solving real-world problems and building practical solutions. summary: Walkback Under Uncertainty estimates the region from which a crew on Mars could still walk back to a habitat within an EVA time budget, and reports how reliable that estimate is when it is computed from coarse terrain data. For a chosen habitat location and time budget, the system predicts a walkback region on a 200 m planner DEM and compares it against a 1 m HiRISE DTM of Jezero crater (held-out truth). We pre-registered our validation plan before analysis and report all results, including a shortfall: at the registered default setting, coverage of the 1 m truth is 0.0% against our 95% target. Diagnostics show why (the start cell is perturbed or blocked in some realizations, and a 200 m staircase DEM gives misleading slopes). The result is a working prototype with an API, a web map, a reliability chart and explicit assumptions. It shows how much trust coarse terrain data deserves in EVA planning. It is not flight software.
details:
LINKS: Live app: https://walkback-rlvz.vercel.app | Source code: https://github.com/Eman2123/Walkback

WHAT IT DOES: Given a habitat location and an EVA time budget, Walkback computes an estimated walkback region using a speed model, a slope cutoff and an 8-connected Dijkstra travel-time search over a coarse DEM. An ensemble of perturbed terrain realizations gives a calibrated region and a reliability measure. Results are validated against a 1 m HiRISE DTM of Jezero crater degraded to the same coarse scale.

HOW WE VALIDATED: Methods were pre-registered (PREREGISTRATION.md) before results were seen. We report coverage, Brier score and reliability bins. The registered default is a shortfall, and we kept it as registered. A labelled post-hoc diagnostic (start cell kept passable) gives 86.9% coverage, still below target. We also found that slope computed on a 200 m staircase DEM is exactly 0 inside blocks, so the registered model scores worse (Brier 0.0157) than a forecast that always says "never steep" (0.0020). Computing slope on the 200 m block grid was an exploratory variant that reaches no-skill level.

WHY IT MATTERS: Mission planning needs to know not only how far a crew can walk but how much to trust a prediction made from coarse terrain data. Our main contribution is an honest, reproducible test of that trust, with failures reported openly.

BUILT WITH: Python, FastAPI, NumPy/GDAL-based terrain pipeline, SQLAlchemy/Alembic, React + Vite + Tailwind CSS, deployed on Vercel. Source is public on GitHub.

LIMITATIONS: Flat-ground speed, slope cutoff and roughness are assumptions. Mars gravity, spacesuit effects, rocks and sand are not modelled. One site (Jezero) only. Nothing here is flight software or a safety claim.

KNOWN WEAKNESSES (reported in our repository): At the registered default setting (model v1), coverage of the 1 m truth is 0.0% (95% CI 0.0% to 0.4%), see reports/validation_report.md; we kept that result as registered. The live app uses model profile v2 (time to the habitat, habitat cell kept passable), which gives 86.9% coverage (95% CI 84.7% to 88.8%) on the Jezero window. That is still below the 95% target, so it is also a shortfall, and it has not yet been tested out of sample on the steep windows. In our extended experiments, false reach (calibrated cells the 1 m truth says are not reachable) reaches up to 57.7% in some variants (reports/validation_extended.csv), and on the steep-P windows the setting that reaches 95% coverage calls 25% to 45% too much area reachable, so high coverage there comes with an optimistic planner. The planner's Brier score (0.0157) is worse than a forecast that always says "never steep" (0.0020). Our next step is to run v2 out of sample on the steeper windows and on a second site, both registered before analysis.

ROUTE CHECK: Area coverage does not show whether the route the planner would choose actually works. We therefore walked the planner's own shortest route on the 1 m truth (pre-registered before it was run, reports/route_feasibility.md). On the Jezero window, 88.8% of the 987 calibrated cells (876) have a route that gets home within the budget; none cross a cell that is impassable in the truth, and 111 are too slow. This is lower than 1 minus the area false reach (92.7%), as expected. It covers one window with almost no steep cells and is not a safety claim.

TEAM: Eman (lead, science and validation), Shela (backend), Urooj (frontend) and Sadia (Research work).
